tema: El hackeo de Twitter de 2020: un chico de 17 años de Florida que tomó las cuentas de Obama, Musk y Apple con una llamada telefónica
titulo: The 17-Year-Old Who Hacked Twitter With a Phone Call
descripcion:
On July 15, 2020, the Twitter accounts of Barack Obama, Elon Musk, Joe Biden, Bill Gates and Apple all started posting the same bitcoin scam at the same time. Within hours, more than one hundred thousand dollars had been sent to the scammers. The mastermind was not a foreign intelligence agency. It was a 17-year-old in Tampa, Florida, and his main weapon was a telephone.

This is the story of how a handful of young hackers talked their way inside one of the most powerful companies on the internet, what investigators found when they followed the money, and the uncomfortable lesson it left for every company and every one of us.

#truecrime #cybersecurity #twitterhack
resumen_es: Documental sobre el hackeo de Twitter del 15 de julio de 2020. Un grupo de jóvenes, liderado por Graham Ivan Clark, de 17 años, engañó por teléfono a empleados de Twitter haciéndose pasar por soporte técnico, entró a la herramienta interna de administración y publicó una estafa de bitcoin desde las cuentas de Obama, Musk, Biden, Gates y Apple, recaudando más de 118 mil dólares. Se cuenta la investigación, las detenciones, las condenas (3 años para Clark, 5 para Joseph O'Connor) y el informe del regulador de Nueva York, que encontró que Twitter no tenía jefe de seguridad. Cierra con la lección: el eslabón más débil de la seguridad son las personas.

escenas.narracion: At around four in the afternoon, on July fifteenth, twenty twenty, Elon Musk's Twitter account posted something strange.
It promised that any bitcoin sent to a certain address would be sent back, doubled. A few minutes later, Bill Gates's account posted almost the same message.
Then Jeff Bezos. Then Barack Obama. Then Joe Biden, Kanye West, Kim Kardashian, and the official accounts of Apple and Uber.
Some of the most powerful accounts on the planet were all running the same scam, at the same time. And nobody at Twitter could stop it.
In the hours that followed, people around the world sent the scammers more than one hundred eighteen thousand dollars in bitcoin.
escenas.subtexto: sent to the scammers in bitcoin

escenas.narracion: Most people assumed it had to be a foreign government, or an elite team of professional criminals. The truth turned out to be much stranger.
The man behind the biggest security breach in Twitter's history was not a man at all. He was a seventeen-year-old from Tampa, Florida.
And he didn't break in with sophisticated code. He used something far more powerful. A phone call.
This is the story of how a group of young hackers talked their way into one of the most important companies on the internet, and why it worked.
Case file. The Twitter heist.
To understand how this happened, we have to go back a few months, to the spring of twenty twenty.
The pandemic had just sent millions of office workers home. Twitter was one of the companies that moved almost its entire staff to remote work.
Suddenly, employees were logging into company systems from their kitchens and living rooms, through a virtual private network, or VPN.
And when that connection failed, they called the IT help desk. Calls from tech support became completely normal.
Inside Twitter, a small number of employees had access to a powerful internal tool. It could change the email address linked to almost any account, reset its security settings, and hand over control.
That tool was the master key to the platform. And according to a later investigation by New York regulators, the company protecting it had a serious gap at the top.
Since December of twenty nineteen, Twitter had not had a chief information security officer. The person whose job was to lead the defense simply wasn't there.
Meanwhile, in a corner of the internet most people never see, a very different community was paying attention.
There are online forums where people buy and sell rare social media usernames. Short handles, like a single letter or a single number, can sell for thousands of dollars.
Some of the people in that world had learned that stealing those accounts was often easier than buying them. And the most effective method rarely involved code.
It involved convincing a real human being to give you access. Security experts call it social engineering.
Graham Ivan Clark knew that world well. And by the summer of twenty twenty, he had a plan that went far beyond stealing a few usernames.
So how do you trick a security-conscious tech company into letting you in? You call them.
According to the New York Department of Financial Services, the attackers phoned Twitter employees, pretending to be from the company's own IT help desk.
They said they were responding to a problem with the VPN. It sounded routine. In the middle of the pandemic, that kind of call happened all the time.
The callers then sent employees to a website that looked exactly like Twitter's real VPN login page. But it was fake.
When an employee typed in their username and password, the hackers used them on the real site, at the same moment.
That triggered a two-factor security request on the employee's phone. And because they believed they were talking to their own IT team, some of them approved it.
Twitter itself later described it in a single sentence.
The social engineering that occurred on July fifteenth targeted a small number of employees through a phone spear phishing attack.
escenas.texto: The social engineering that occurred on July 15, 2020, targeted a small number of employees through a phone spear phishing attack.

escenas.narracion: With those credentials, the attackers eventually reached employees who had access to the internal tool. The master key was now in the hands of a teenager.
At first, they used it the way that community always had. According to federal prosecutors, access to valuable usernames was offered for sale.
Then they went bigger. Accounts of cryptocurrency companies started posting the bitcoin offer. And then came the most famous names on the platform.
New York regulators found that the hackers logged into one hundred thirty accounts, and sent tweets from forty five of them.
Inside Twitter, engineers scrambled. With no quick way to know which accounts were compromised, the company took a drastic step.
For several hours, it blocked many verified accounts from tweeting at all. Presidents, celebrities and news organizations went silent.
That night, Twitter's chief executive, Jack Dorsey, posted a short message.
Tough day for us at Twitter. We all feel terrible this happened.
escenas.texto: Tough day for us at Twitter. We all feel terrible this happened.

escenas.narracion: The hackers had pulled off something extraordinary. But they had made one critical mistake. They had stolen money in a way that leaves a permanent trail.
Every bitcoin transaction is recorded on a public ledger, forever. Investigators followed the payments, and connected them to accounts, emails and devices.
Just sixteen days after the attack, on July thirty first, police arrested Graham Ivan Clark in Tampa. He faced thirty felony charges.
The same day, federal prosecutors charged two other young men, Mason Sheppard in the United Kingdom, and Nima Fazeli in Orlando, Florida, for their alleged roles.
A third, Joseph O'Connor, a British man known online as PlugWalkJoe, was arrested in Spain in twenty twenty one, and later extradited to the United States.
In March of twenty twenty one, Clark accepted a plea deal. Because he was a minor at the time, he was sentenced as a youthful offender.
Three years in a juvenile prison, followed by three years of probation. If he violates that probation, he faces a minimum of ten years in adult prison.
escenas.subtexto: in juvenile prison for the mastermind

escenas.narracion: O'Connor received a heavier sentence. In June of twenty twenty three, a federal judge in New York sentenced him to five years in prison, for the Twitter hack and other crimes.
Months later, New York regulators published their report. Their conclusion was blunt. The hack succeeded because Twitter's security had not kept up with its importance.
They called for a dedicated regulator for the largest social media companies, arguing that platforms this powerful could no longer be treated like ordinary apps.
But the real lesson of this story is simpler, and it applies to all of us. The most sophisticated security system in the world can be undone by one convincing phone call.
Nobody here exploited a brilliant software flaw. They exploited trust, routine, and the pressure of a strange moment in history.
So if you ever get a call from tech support, your bank, or anyone asking you to approve a login, stop. Hang up, and call them back on a number you know is real.
And never approve a security prompt that you didn't start yourself. That single habit would have stopped this entire attack.
